items.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid development of large language models (LLMs) has revived, in new forms, classical questions concerning meaning, understanding, and the originality of thought. Much of the debate, however, is affected by the difficulty of operationally defining concepts such as consciousness or free will, whose application even to human beings remains philosophically controversial. This paper proposes to narrow the problem to a more limited question that is amenable to experimental testing: whether an LLM can produce original semantic content while operating within a domain specifically created after its training. To this end, we propose the use of what we shall call synthetic jurisdictions: artificial legal systems constructed ad hoc and characterised by arbitrary rules, open-textured concepts, normative ambiguities, gaps, and designed antinomies. In contrast to traditional rule-following and rule-induction benchmarks, the protocol seeks to distinguish the application of rules and the reconstruction of an underlying generative structure from the construction of new principles and norms capable of guiding further cases.</jats:p>
title: Synthetic Jurisdictions as a Testbed for Semantic Originality in Large Language Models: An Experimental Design Proposal

items.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid development of large language models (LLMs) has revived, in new forms, classical questions concerning meaning, understanding, and the originality of thought. Much of the debate, however, is affected by the difficulty of operationally defining concepts such as consciousness or free will, whose application even to human beings remains philosophically controversial. This paper proposes to narrow the problem to a more limited question that is amenable to experimental testing: whether an LLM can produce original semantic content while operating within a domain specifically created after its training. To this end, we propose the use of what we shall call synthetic jurisdictions: artificial legal systems constructed ad hoc and characterised by arbitrary rules, open-textured concepts, normative ambiguities, gaps, and designed antinomies. In contrast to traditional rule-following and rule-induction benchmarks, the protocol seeks to distinguish the application of rules and the reconstruction of an underlying generative structure from the construction of new principles and norms capable of guiding further cases. An exploratory proof of concept was conducted with Claude in a source-closed synthetic jurisdiction. Across a six-case sequence, each decision was incorporated as an internal precedent for the next; a lexical-scramble replication of the first case preserved the jurisdiction's normative structure while replacing its operative vocabulary. The outputs produced source-grounded, legally intelligible candidate constructions, including interpretive criteria concerning identity, effective refusal, derivative images, and collective memory. The proof of concept is illustrative rather than confirmatory: it does not establish model-level performance or semantic originality, but demonstrates the practical feasibility of the protocol and motivates a preregistered evaluation with independent legal assessors.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Digital transformation drives organizations to seek operational efficiency through process automation. Robotic Process Automation (RPA) has consolidated as a solution for repetitive tasks but presents a critical bottleneck in the discovery and documentation phase, consuming up to 40% of total project time and heavily relying on scarce human specialists. Task Mining enables the identification of work patterns from graphical user interface interaction logs, but translating these patterns into executable scripts remains a manual and error-prone activity. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer code generation capabilities but present hallucination risks when directly applied in critical systems. This paper presents the ORBITA Framework (Orchestrated Recommender Based on Intelligent Task Analysis), a six-layer architecture combining Task Mining and LLMs mediated by Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to recommend automations with sandbox validation and mandatory human governance. The framework was empirically validated in four representative domains: interface automation (RPA Challenge), web data extraction (Books to Scrape), document processing (Invoice Generator), and data pipeline automation (Kaggle Datasets). Results demonstrated an average 97.3% reduction in Mean Automation Time compared to manual development, with a 100% rate of functionally executable scripts after structural validation. </jats:p>
title: Um framework de recomendação de automação baseado em Task Mining e Large Language Models
ORBITA: An automation recommendation framework based on Task Mining and Large Language Models
